nj_charity_care.applies_to: all NJ acute care hospitals, hospital care only (not physician/anesthesia/radiology reading/outpatient Rx)

wa_charity_care.applies_to: all WA acute care hospitals -- patient responsibility portion of hospital charges
wa_charity_care.note: RCW 70.170.060(5) sets TWO schedules: a more generous one for larger hospital systems/hospitals (defined by owning 3+ acute hospitals, or specific large hospitals in King County or a southern-border county), and this floor schedule required of every other hospital. CareMap doesn't have hospital bed-count/ownership-network data loaded to tell which hospitals qualify for the larger-system schedule, so this is the legal MINIMUM every WA hospital must offer -- some hospitals are required to offer better terms (up to 400% FPL). Confirm with the specific hospital.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: unconfirmed -- the statute's income-based eligibility doesn't explicitly require uninsured status the way NJ's does; applied conservatively here (same uninsured-only gate as NJ) pending fuller verification
eligibility.not_medicaid_eligible: unconfirmed -- hospitals must help Medicaid-eligible patients apply for Medicaid first, but the statute doesn't flatly exclude them from charity care the way NJ's does

il_charity_care.source: https://codes.findlaw.com/il/chapter-210-health-facilities-and-regulation/il-st-sect-210-89-10/ (210 ILCS 89/10 and 89/5, Hospital Uninsured Patient Discount Act)
il_charity_care.applies_to: all IL hospitals -- uninsured patients only (the statute does not mention underinsured patients at all, unlike NJ/WA)
il_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current codified text (210 ILCS 89/5 and /10). Below the free-care threshold, patient_pays_pct is a real, exact 0% -- no gap there. ABOVE it, the law does NOT set a clean percentage: the discount is charges x (1 - cost_to_charge_ratio x 1.35), a real statutory formula, but it needs each hospital's own Medicare cost-to-charge ratio, which CareMap doesn't have loaded (it's a different CMS dataset -- cost reports -- not the Hospital General Information / DRG charge data already in use). A hard cap also applies there: a hospital can never collect more than 20% of the patient's family income in any 12-month period, regardless of the formula result. CareMap deliberately shows NO percentage above the free-care threshold rather than guess one -- only the free-care floor and the 20%-income-cap fact are real without that missing data.

ny_charity_care.source: https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PBH/2807-K (NY Public Health Law 2807-k(9) and (9-a), Hospital Financial Assistance Law, amended 2024-04-20)
ny_charity_care.applies_to: all NY general hospitals -- uninsured AND underinsured patients (unlike IL, which is uninsured-only)
ny_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current codified text (PBH 2807-k(9-a), post-2024-04-20 amendment -- an older DOH advisory letter citing a 300% FPL ceiling is stale; the current ceiling is 400%). Below the free-care threshold, patient_pays_pct is a real, exact 0% -- 'no nominal payment shall be collected' per the statute itself. ABOVE it, the law does NOT discount a percentage of billed charges the way NJ/WA/IL do: it caps payment at 10% (201-300% FPL) or 20% (301-400% FPL) of the MEDICAID-EQUIVALENT rate for the service, a completely different dollar base than the typical billed charge CareMap has from CMS Medicare Inpatient by Provider and Service. CareMap has no Medicaid-rate data loaded at all, so there isn't even a disclosable cap fact to surface above the threshold the way IL's 20%-of-income cap is (that one needs no extra dataset; NY's does). CareMap deliberately shows NO percentage and NO cap fact above the free-care threshold -- only the free-care floor is real without Medicaid-rate data. Above 400% FPL the statute is silent (hospital's own policy).

eligibility.not_medicaid_eligible: unconfirmed -- immigration/documentation status is explicitly barred as a criterion (9-a(a)), but the statute doesn't flatly exclude Medicaid-eligible patients the way NJ's does

or_charity_care.applies_to: Oregon NONPROFIT hospitals only (ORS 442.612(8): organized under ORS chapter 65 or IRC 501(c)) -- excludes for-profit and government-owned hospitals. CareMap gates this via CMS's own 'ownership' field (Voluntary non-profit - *): see charity_care_participant in build_data.py.
or_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current codified text (ORS 442.610-442.618). Unlike IL/NY/CO, Oregon's dollar base is real billed charges (ORS 442.612(9): 'patient's cost' = charges billed net of insurance/public-program reimbursement) -- the exact CMS billed-charge figure CareMap already has, so the full sliding scale is computable, not just a free floor. These are statutory MINIMUM discounts (a hospital's own policy may be more generous, never less) -- same floor-schedule pattern as WA's RCW 70.170.060(5)(b), so patient_pays_pct here is the maximum a patient is guaranteed NOT to exceed, not a guessed exact figure. No uninsured/underinsured restriction found in the statute -- broader than every other state modeled (covers insured, underinsured, uninsured alike), but CareMap still only shows a charity-care price to the uninsured per the conservative gate applied everywhere else, since insured patients have a separate relevant number (their own cost-sharing) this app doesn't model.

eligibility.must_be_un_or_underinsured: not required by the statute itself (income-only test) -- applied conservatively here anyway, consistent with every other modeled state

md_charity_care.applies_to: every MD hospital under HSCRC (Health Services Cost Review Commission) jurisdiction -- virtually all MD acute care hospitals, regardless of ownership, under Maryland's unique all-payer rate-setting system
md_charity_care.note: Verified directly against the current codified text. One real wrinkle: the statute discounts the patient's 'out-of-pocket expense for the regulated hospital service', not 'charges' by name. For an INSURED patient that would mean something net of insurer payment -- but CareMap only ever shows a charity-care price to the UNINSURED (same conservative gate as every other state here), and for an uninsured patient there's no insurer payment to net against, so out-of-pocket expense collapses to the full regulated rate -- which, under Maryland's all-payer system, is the same rate CMS's own Medicare Inpatient by Provider and Service dataset reports for MD hospitals (unlike most states, Maryland's regulated rate and its Medicare-reported rate aren't materially different by design). This is an inference from the uninsured-only restriction, not a literal statutory statement that the base is 'billed charges' -- treated here the same honest way as WA's unconfirmed eligibility gate. Maryland also has a separate hardship tier (medical debt exceeding 25% of family income over 12 months, up to 500% FPL) that CareMap can't verify (needs the patient's actual debt history) and does not compute.

eligibility.asset_limit_note: may only count household monetary assets over $100,000 (19-214.1(b)(8)(i)), excluding certain retirement assets -- more generous than NJ's $7,500/$15,000

good_faith_estimate.applies_to: uninsured or self-pay patients scheduling care at least 3 business days ahead
